title: AI Scribe or Templates? What Each One Writes in a Vet Clinic
summary: A veterinary AI scribe writes your SOAP notes; templates save the rest. See what each tool actually writes across a typical day in practice.
body_markdown:
## Where the typing in a clinic actually goes


An AI scribe turns the conversation in the exam room into a medical record, but it does not write discharge instructions, refill replies, updates for the pet owner, or front-desk messages. To see where the typing burden really lies in a veterinary practice, look at how much text is produced outside the exam room on a typical day. This is the stream of communication a busy small-animal practice generates between 8 a.m. and close:


- Post-op and dental discharge instructions, bundled with the medication list and monitoring paragraphs
- The vaccine reaction notice that goes out with a wellness visit
- The “Your pet is awake and doing great” message when a patient recovers from anesthesia
- Phone callback notes and communication logs between the pet owner and the vet
- Reminders, front-desk confirmations, and pre-anesthetic instructions sent the night before surgery


## What an AI scribe covers: the conversation in the room


Generative AI scribes have earned their place in the exam room. The vet talks to the pet owner as usual while the scribe listens and writes the subjective and objective sections: what the pet owner reported and what was found during the examination. The transcribed text is then structured into the medical record.


AI scribes have been especially helpful for general practitioners with busy appointment schedules. Clinicians who use ambient veterinary scribes often report a noticeable drop in their end-of-day backlog. Instead of sitting in a quiet office for two hours trying to reconstruct six different physical exams from memory, they find the drafts already waiting in their practice management software.


Audio quality varies from room to room, and drafting style differs across software. But the main function stays the same: the AI scribe filters out small talk from the clinical dialogue and produces a draft in standard medical format, so the doctor can focus on the patient rather than the keyboard during the exam.


## What still gets typed by hand


A veterinary team’s typing isn’t confined to the exam room. Much of the administrative work happens in the treatment area, the pharmacy, or at the front desk, places where there is no conversation for a scribe to listen to.


Think about the documents created outside the exam room. A technician could spend 10 minutes drafting a dental discharge sheet, soft-food instructions, or an anesthesia recovery note. A receptionist might spend the morning answering refill requests while explaining to three different clients that their pet needs a physical exam before a new prescription can be authorized. A technician might also text a client to let them know their dog is awake after a spay and doing well.


These documents and communications have one thing in common: their content repeats nearly word for word. Every patient’s medical record is different, but a vaccine reaction warning or a bland-diet instruction sheet looks the same every time it is sent.


Many of these records live in the clinic’s practice management software (PIMS). But a template inside a PIMS stays inside the PIMS. It can’t be used in a browser-based texting platform, a web-based email system, or an online pharmacy portal. When communication moves outside the PIMS, the team is left to copy and paste from it or type the whole paragraph by hand.


## You still review every record: why fixed wording for the normal parts helps


Clinics that use a scribe share the same workflow: the tool generates a draft, and the doctor reads it, corrects any mistakes, and signs it. Veterinarians who use AI scribes swear by them, but they also recommend reviewing every draft. It’s not uncommon for these tools to mishear a term or mix up who said what. Every practice has a favorite draft that went sideways badly enough to laugh about in the break room. The doctor is still the one who checks and adjusts the record.


The review itself becomes a repetitive bottleneck. Whether the vet is standardizing a treatment plan or fixing a misheard finding, the corrections follow familiar patterns. Vets end up typing the same physical exam phrasing or the same standard diagnostic plan again and again to fix what the AI produced.


Having that fixed wording a few keystrokes away cuts the time it takes to correct a draft. This is where Text Blaze fits in. A vet can type a shortcut such as /normalpe to drop the clinic’s standard normal physical exam wording into the draft and speed up the review. Vets can save their own phrasing or start from ready-made templates, and a pop-up lets them fill in the details that change for each patient.


## Using both: a worked example of one appointment


Here’s how a veterinary AI scribe and saved snippets work together during a routine appointment for a senior dog with a hind-end limp.


**Before the visit.** The day before the appointment, the receptionist types a shortcut to fill in the appointment confirmation and arrival instructions and sends them through the clinic’s texting platform. There is no exam conversation yet, so the scribe has nothing to do here.


**In the exam room.** The veterinary technician takes the dog’s history. The vet examines the dog while the AI scribe listens to the whole conversation and drafts the subjective and objective sections of the SOAP note.


**Reviewing the draft.** The vet reads the draft and uses a shortcut to replace the scribe’s wording with the clinic’s standard normal findings for the unaffected body systems. Next, the vet fills in the Text Blaze pop-up with this dog’s joint findings and range of motion, leaves the rest as is, and signs the record. The review takes a handful of minutes, and the edits are nearly the same in every lameness workup.


**Discharge.** The technician prepares the discharge: the anti-inflammatory dose and timing, activity limits, the recheck date, and the paragraph on what to watch for at home. Typing all of that by hand would take several minutes, but the technician pulls up the template with a shortcut from the free[Veterinary Discharge Instructions & Client Handout Templates](https://text.blaze.today/marketplace/templates/veterinary-discharge-client-handout-templates) and fills in the details.


**Follow-up.** Two days later, the receptionist sends an email to the owner to check on the dog’s response to the new joint supplement.


The scribe covered the exam room. The other four steps of this appointment, the repetitive paperwork and client communication, were handled by saved snippets and keyboard shortcuts.

## Frequently asked questions


### Do I still need templates if I use a veterinary AI scribe?


Yes, for all the text that lives outside the medical record. The AI scribe drafts the clinical chart from what is said in the exam room. The discharge sheet, client messages, refill replies, and callback notes are often written by someone who wasn’t in the exam room, and that text repeats nearly word for word between patients. That repetition is exactly what templates solve, by keeping the wording ready under simple keyboard shortcuts.


### Do AI scribes replace templates for veterinarians?


They replace most of the manual typing of the clinical record itself, not the communication around the visit. Everything a client receives, such as the go-home sheet or the refill reply, is written outside the exam and repeats across patients. That’s why most clinics using AI scribes still keep saved wording for discharges and client communication, and why the two tools work side by side rather than one replacing the other.
